traveler: Anita Garibaldi (Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro)
title: The Lagoon to the Marsh: the Farrapos, the Plata, and the Retreat from Rome
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Laguna, the Coast She Was Married Off On

stops.name: Laguna, birth above the lagoon
stops.date_confidence: attested: 30 August 1821, given identically by the Portuguese and English accounts; the birthplace is Morrinhos, in the Laguna district, today a neighbourhood of Tubarao rather than of Laguna.
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of August, at Morrinhos above the lagoon town of Laguna, Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro is born to Bento Ribeiro da Silva and Maria Antônia de Jesus Antunes. The coast here is a country of fishermen, cattle drovers and salt water, the southern rim of the Empire of Brazil and the northern rim of the gaucho world that Hernando Arias de Saavedra's mozos perdidos had begun two centuries earlier. Her father dies while she is a girl and the household falls into want. The day of birth is documented; almost nothing else about the childhood is.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Santo Antônio dos Anjos da Laguna, Santa Catarina

stops.name: Laguna, married at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested by pt.wikipedia to her fourteenth birthday, 30 August 1835, in the Igreja Matriz Santo Antônio dos Anjos.
stops.campa: On her fourteenth birthday she is married in the Igreja Matriz Santo Antônio dos Anjos to Manuel Duarte de Aguiar, a shoemaker. Her mother arranges it; the Portuguese account calls the marriage forced. It produces no children and no household worth the name. Three weeks later, in Rio Grande do Sul, the Guerra dos Farrapos opens against the Empire, a republican rebellion that will run ten years. It reaches this coast by sea four years later, and she is still in the town when it does.
suggested_refs: The Igreja Matriz de Santo Antônio dos Anjos, Laguna

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the letter of marque
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1837 by pt.wikipedia 'Guerra dos Farrapos'; no month or day is given, and the date defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: Giuseppe Garibaldi, condemned to death in Piedmont and sailing under other men's flags, is held in Rio de Janeiro and there meets Bento Gonçalves, president of the rebel Rio-Grandense republic. Gonçalves gives him a letter of marque against Imperial shipping: legal cover for piracy in the service of a republic with no navy. On the first of September 1838 he is commissioned captain-lieutenant and commander of the Farroupilha fleet, a fleet that does not yet exist. He is thirty. Anita is sixteen, on a coast eight hundred kilometres south, and has never heard of him.
suggested_refs: The Farroupilha letters of marque issued by Bento Gonçalves da Silva

stops.name: Laguna, the husband goes to the Imperial army
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: en.wikipedia dates the departure only to a range of about 1837-1838; the year here is a midpoint and the month and day default to 1 January.
stops.campa: Manuel Duarte de Aguiar leaves Laguna to enlist in the Imperial army and does not come back. Whether he abandons the marriage or is swept up by the levy the sources do not say; the English account calls it abandonment and gives no date closer than a two-year range. Ana Maria is sixteen or seventeen, married, alone, and living in a town that the rebellion to the south is about to reach from the water. Nothing in the record places her outside Laguna before the year the war arrives.
suggested_refs: Imperial Brazilian army muster rolls for Santa Catarina, 1837-1839

segments.name: The Corsair Fleet and the Taking of Laguna

stops.name: Camaquã, the shipyard with no walls
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1839 by pt.wikipedia 'Guerra dos Farrapos'; no month is given and the date defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: On the Camaquã river, in the marsh country west of the Lagoa dos Patos, Garibaldi and Luigi Rossetti build the republic's navy out of nothing: two war launches laid down at a yard with no walls. Francisco Pedro de Abreu, the officer the war calls Moringue, comes at them with more than a hundred men; Garibaldi entrenches some fourteen workers and holds the ground. The Rio-Grandense republic has no port and no coast it can keep, and everything it will ever do at sea begins here, in a shipyard defended by carpenters.
suggested_refs: The Farroupilha shipyard on the Rio Camaquã, Rio Grande do Sul

stops.name: Laguna, the town taken from the sea
stops.date_confidence: attested: 22 July 1839 for the capture. The proclamation of the República Juliana is dated 29 July by pt.wikipedia 'República Juliana' and 24 July by pt.wikipedia 'Museu Anita Garibaldi'; the contradiction is left open.
stops.campa: Farroupilha forces under Davi Canabarro take Laguna while the flotilla holds the bar, and within the week the República Juliana is proclaimed in the town: a second rebel republic, aligned with the Rio-Grandense one to the south, with a harbour at last. The Empire has lost the only port on this stretch of coast. Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro, married and abandoned, is inside the town when a republic is declared over her head, and the man who commands its ships is standing offshore looking at the houses.
stops.quote: I one day cast a casual glance at a house in the Burra, (the eastern part of the entrance of the Jayuna,) and there observed a young female whose appearance struck me as having something very extraordinary.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (New York, 1861), Ch. IX; the translation renders her name 'Anna' throughout the chapter
suggested_refs: The proclamation of the República Juliana, Laguna, July 1839
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Laguna, the meeting
stops.date_confidence: contested: pt.wikipedia dates the meeting 22 July 1839; en.wikipedia dates her joining him to October 1839. She is seventeen in July and turns eighteen on 30 August 1839, so the widely repeated 'then eighteen' holds only for the October dating. The two accounts are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: He comes ashore and finds her. She is seventeen, weeks from her eighteenth birthday; he is thirty-two, condemned to death in his own country, commanding a rebel flotilla for a republic that will not outlive the year. His memoirs give the sentence he says he spoke on sight, before either of them knew anything else about the other: a claim rather than a courtship. He writes that with those words alone he had made a knot which only death could untie, and death takes ten years to get to it.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, Vita e memorie di Giuseppe Garibaldi, ed. Alexandre Dumas (Milan, 1860), verified in the scanned text at archive.org, identifier bub_gb_KdPZtNeocooC; 'Maiden, thou shalt be mine.' Italian Wikipedia gives the variant 'Devi essere mia' from Le memorie di Garibaldi (Milan, 1860), p. 76. The line is absent from the Dwight translation of 1861.
suggested_refs: Vita e memorie di Giuseppe Garibaldi, ed. Alexandre Dumas, Milan 1860

stops.name: Laguna harbour, aboard the Rio Pardo
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia to 20 October 1839; the Portuguese chronology has her with him from July, and the discrepancy is unresolved.
stops.campa: She goes aboard the brigantine Rio Pardo in the harbour, with the flotilla fitting out for corsair work along the Santa Catarina coast. She is a married woman leaving a husband who has already left her, in a Catholic town, in front of everyone who has known her since birth. No ceremony is performed and no arrangement is made; she walks up the plank in daylight and stays aboard. From this day she is a combatant, and every place she appears in the record for the next ten years is a place an army is moving through.
stops.quote: I saluted her; we were soon acquainted; and I found that the hidden treasure which I had discovered was of rare and inestimable worth.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. IX
suggested_refs: The Farroupilha brigantine Rio Pardo, Laguna, October 1839
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Imbituba, the first shot
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1839; en.wikipedia gives 15 November for the naval battle of Laguna and Imbituba, while Garibaldi's own memoir places an action off this coast during the corsair cruise without a date.
stops.campa: Off Imbituba the flotilla meets Imperial warships. Anita is on deck, refuses to be put ashore, and works the guns; Garibaldi's account has her firing the opening shot with her own hand and shouting at the men who hesitate. The Brazilians call her the Amazon. She has been aboard a matter of weeks. Garibaldi writes the scene down eleven years later in New York, still calling her incomparable, and every account since takes it from him. Brazil and Italy both keep the match in her hand.
stops.quote: my wife, the incomparable Anita, fired the first shot, putting the match to the gun with her own hand, and animating with her voice the timid and the hesitating.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. X; the one place in the memoir where the translator spells her name 'Anita' rather than 'Anna'
suggested_refs: The naval action off Imbituba, Santa Catarina, November 1839
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Laguna, the republic broken
stops.date_confidence: attested: 15 November 1839. The operation is credited by pt.wikipedia 'República Juliana' to General Francisco José de Sousa Soares de Andrea, not to Frederico Mariath, who commanded naval elements in the campaign.
stops.campa: Imperial forces retake Laguna: more than three thousand men by land and a fleet of thirteen ships by sea, under Soares de Andrea, with the rebel vessels already found and destroyed at the mouth of the Rio Maciambu before the assault comes. The República Juliana has lasted under four months. The ammunition is landed under fire and Anita carries the orders through it, back and forth between deck and shore. She leaves the coast she was born on with the retreating column and never sees it again.
stops.quote: I had sent Anna with the message, directing her to remain on shore; but she returned on board with the answer, showing a coolness and courage which excited my astonishment and highest admiration. To her boldness and exertions was due the saving of the ammunition, which was safely landed.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. X
suggested_refs: The recapture of Laguna, 15 November 1839, and the end of the República Juliana
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Lages, Christmas in the highlands
stops.date_confidence: traditional: pt.wikipedia places the retreating column at Lages at Christmas 1839; no document is cited for the halt.
stops.campa: The column climbs out of the coastal plain into the serra catarinense and passes Christmas at Lages, a cattle town on high grassland where the roads are mud and the nights are cold. Behind them the Empire holds the coast; ahead lie the Rio Grande do Sul border and a republic already losing its war. Anita rides with the men, dressed as they are. She is pregnant. The grass country she is crossing is the same corridor the drovers and the deserters ride the length of the continent, and the retreat has eighteen days left to run.
suggested_refs: The colonial cattle road through Lages and the serra catarinense

stops.name: Curitibanos, taken prisoner
stops.date_confidence: attested for the action of 12 January 1840 and for her capture; the escape that follows is flagged as traditional in the English account and is carried as legend by the Portuguese one.
stops.campa: Imperial troops fall on the column at Curitibanos and break it. Anita, pregnant, is cut off from Garibaldi in the fighting and taken prisoner. The Portuguese account has her asking her captors' leave to walk the field for his body and going among the dead until she is satisfied he is not there. Having established that he is alive, she leaves. Tradition holds that she takes a horse and rides straight out through the lines. The escape is legend before it is anything else, and the English account says as much.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Curitibanos, Santa Catarina, January 1840

stops.name: Rio Canoas, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: dated only to January 1840, immediately after the escape; the day is inferred and the ford itself is reconstructed from the country rather than named in any source.
stops.campa: She reaches the Rio Canoas with pursuit behind her and no boat. The account every version of her keeps is this one: pregnant, alone, hunted, she puts the horse into the water and swims the river. What is attested is a crossing. The exact ford is reconstruction, and the swim comes down through tradition rather than through any paper written at the time. It is the episode the whole legend of her endurance stands on, and it is the episode with the least evidence under it.
suggested_refs: The Rio Canoas above Curitibanos, crossing point of the January 1840 escape

stops.name: Vacaria, the reunion
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: pt.wikipedia gives eight days alone in the campo between the escape and the reunion but no date; late January or February 1840, defaulted here to the first of the month.
stops.campa: Eight days alone in open country, wounded and without food, and she comes into Vacaria and finds Garibaldi, who has been told she is dead. Family tradition holds that Menotti's skull was deformed by a fall she took from the horse during this flight, and that the child is born marked by the escape. She is eighteen, seven months from her first childbirth, and she has crossed a war on horseback and on foot to get back to a man she has known for six months. The Brazilian towns that carry her name carry it because of these eight days.
stops.quote: My wife was my treasure, and no less fervent in the cause of the people than myself; and she looked upon battles as an amusement, and the inconveniences of a life in the field as a pastime.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. X
suggested_refs: The campo of Vacaria, Rio Grande do Sul, reached alone after eight days
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

segments.name: Rio Grande do Sul, the Child in the Saddle

stops.name: Piratini, the capital of the Farrapos
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: her presence in Piratini is inferred from Garibaldi's corps operating in the republic's service during 1840, not documented; the month is a placement, not a record.
stops.campa: Piratini is the capital of the Rio-Grandense republic, a town of low white houses on the southern grass that has declared itself a nation and printed the declaration. Garibaldi's corps operates in its service and the couple pass through in the campaigning of that year. The republic has a president, an army, a flag and a war it is losing; what it does not have is a coast, which is why Anita was standing in Laguna the summer before. The Farrapos will hold out five more years and then be folded back into the Empire on terms.
suggested_refs: The casa da câmara of Piratini, seat of the Rio-Grandense republic

stops.name: Mostardas, Menotti born in the field
stops.date_confidence: attested by pt.wikipedia to 16 September 1840, in the field during the Rio Grande do Sul campaign.
stops.campa: On the sand strip between the Lagoa dos Patos and the sea, with the column, Anita gives birth to a son. They name him Menotti, after Ciro Menotti, hanged by the Austrians at Modena nine years before Garibaldi ever saw Brazil. The name is a piece of a war on the far side of the Atlantic carried into a Brazilian cattle district by a Genoese corsair and given to a child born to a girl from Laguna. It is her first childbirth and it happens inside a retreat. Twelve days later the camp is attacked.
suggested_refs: The rancho at Mostardas where Menotti Garibaldi was born, September 1840

stops.name: Near Mostardas, Moringue falls on the camp
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: dated twelve days after Menotti's birth of 16 September 1840, so about 28 September. Garibaldi's memoir names the camp as near San Simon, which is not Mostardas; the pin is placed on the district where the column then lay.
stops.campa: Moringue surprises the camp. Anita is put on a horse with a twelve-day-old baby in her arms and rides out through a storm while the fighting goes on behind her. Garibaldi's own sketch of her records it in a single clause and moves on, the way soldiers record the ordinary. The Empire has been hunting this column for a year, and the child is carried through the hunt in cloth against her body. The family tradition that the Curitibanos fall marked his skull is spoken of in the same breath as this ride.
stops.quote: taking my wife with them, who mounted the saddle, to avoid the enemy, with her infant, then only twelve days old, although it was in the midst of the storm.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. XIII; the passage sits inside Chapter XIII, not Chapter XIV as sometimes cited
suggested_refs: The Moringue raid on Garibaldi's camp, Rio Grande do Sul, September 1840
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Mata das Antas, the forest and the child
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Garibaldi's memoir places the retreat through the woods of Las Antas when the child is about three months old, so around December 1840; the coordinate is placed on the serra route the column took and not on a documented camp.
stops.campa: The column crosses the forest the memoir calls Las Antas when the child is three months old, and Menotti is nearly lost in it. Garibaldi's sketch says the boy was saved with difficulty and as if by a miracle, and that Anna was much distressed, which is as close to fear as any surviving account of her comes. The Farroupilha war is going badly everywhere. Within months the family will be out of Brazil, and the cause she joined at eighteen will be one she survives rather than one she wins.
stops.quote: Anna was much distressed by the apprehension of losing her little son, Menotti, who was saved with difficulty, and as if by a miracle.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. XIV
suggested_refs: The forest crossing of Las Antas in Garibaldi's Brazilian memoir
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Montevideo, the crossing to Uruguay
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1841 by both the English and Portuguese accounts; no month is given and the date defaults to 1 January.
stops.campa: With the Farroupilha cause failing, Anita, Garibaldi and the infant Menotti leave Brazil and come into Montevideo. He trades, keeps a school, and keeps his hand in the politics of the Italian exile. This is the city where San Martín, twelve years earlier, waited two months at anchor and refused the dictatorship of Buenos Aires rather than draw his sword on his own countrymen, and where Alvear had taken the walls for the revolution in 1814. The Plata is where the losers of upriver wars come to wait for the next one.
suggested_refs: The Italian emigration in Montevideo, 1841-1848

stops.name: Iglesia de San Francisco de Asís, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested by pt.wikipedia to 26 March 1842 at the Church of San Francisco de Asís; en.wikipedia gives 1842 without agreeing on the day. Coordinates are those of the church in the Ciudad Vieja per es.wikipedia.
stops.campa: In the church of San Francisco de Asís in the Ciudad Vieja they are married, about three years after Laguna, with Menotti already walking. The first husband is somewhere in the Imperial army; no annulment appears in any record reachable here, and whether Duarte de Aguiar was alive that March no source consulted can say. The marriage is performed anyway. She becomes, in Uruguayan and then Italian paper, Anita Garibaldi, and the name she was baptised with stops being used by anyone except Brazilian historians.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of the Iglesia de San Francisco de Asís, Montevideo, March 1842
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Iglesia de San Francisco de Asís (Montevideo)'

stops.name: Cerrito de la Victoria, the Sitio Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested: the siege opens in 1843 and runs nine years. Anita's own part in the fighting of 1847 is asserted by en.wikipedia and nowhere detailed; treat the participation claim as unelaborated.
stops.campa: Manuel Oribe, Rosas's ally, invests Montevideo from this hill and does not leave for nine years. Inside the walls are the Argentine exiles, the French and Italian legions, and Garibaldi. Juan Manuel de Rosas runs the war from Buenos Aires; Sarmiento comes through and finds his own Facundo already being read in the cafés. Alvear had commanded the siege lines under this same hill in 1814, for the other side of the same argument. Anita is inside the city for the whole of it, and the English account puts her in the defence of 1847 without saying what she did.
suggested_refs: The Cerrito de la Victoria, Oribe's headquarters through the Sitio Grande

stops.name: Montevideo, three children and a grave
stops.date_confidence: attested: Rosita born 1843 and dead at about two in 1845; Teresita born 1845, whose lifespan en.wikipedia gives as 1845-1903; Ricciotti born 1847, given as 1847-1924. The stop is placed at the middle year.
stops.campa: Rosita is born in 1843 and dies of a throat infection at about two years old. Teresita is born in 1845 and Ricciotti in 1847. Anita keeps a household in a city under siege, with a husband commanding foreign volunteers outside the walls, and buries a daughter in it. The red shirts of the Italian Legion, which will become the uniform of a century of insurrection, are cut in Montevideo in these years. She is in her early twenties and has borne four children, of whom three live. These are the years the biographies pass over fastest.
suggested_refs: The Montevideo parish registers of the Garibaldi children, 1843-1847

stops.name: Montevideo, sailing for Nice
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia to January 1848 for the departure; the day is not given and defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Word comes of revolution in Europe. Anita sails first, with the three children, for Nice; Garibaldi follows with his legionaries. She has never seen Italy, does not speak the language of the country she is sailing to, and is going there to hand her children to a mother-in-law she has never met. She leaves the Plata at twenty-six having fought in two wars in it. The ship carries the Brazilian woman of the Farrapos into the Risorgimento, and the Risorgimento gives her eighteen months.
suggested_refs: The 1848 return of the Italian Legion from Montevideo to Europe

stops.name: Nice, the mother-in-law's house
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: she sails from Montevideo in January 1848 and the sources consulted give no arrival date; the month here is an inference from the passage, not a record.
stops.campa: She lands in Nice with Menotti, Teresita and Ricciotti and meets Rosa Raimondi Garibaldi, her husband's mother, for the first time. The children are left in that house. Nice is a Piedmontese town, and Garibaldi is a man under sentence of death returning to the state that passed it, in a year when every capital in Europe is burning. He goes to the war in Lombardy. Anita, who has not waited anywhere since she was seventeen, waits, and that waiting is the only stretch of her adult life the record leaves nearly blank.
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi family house in Nice, where the three children were left

stops.name: Rieti, she rides to the legion
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia to 24 February 1849: 'Qui Anita lo raggiunse il 24 febbraio 1849, dopo aver lasciato i figli a Nizza.' The English article does not mention Rieti at all.
stops.campa: The Roman Republic has been proclaimed in February and Garibaldi is at Rieti with his legion, mustering to march on Rome. Anita leaves the children in Nice and rides down to him. She is twenty-seven. There is no record that anyone asked her to come and none that anyone tried to stop her. From Rieti she goes where the legion goes, which is south to a city that has just abolished the temporal power of the Pope and will hold it abolished for four months and a week.
suggested_refs: The mustering of Garibaldi's legion at Rieti, February 1849

stops.name: Trastevere, the wounded and the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for her presence in Rome from the arrival of the French troops on 30 April 1849; it.wikipedia has her occupied with the wounded and does not place her in combat. Her fighting on the Janiculum is Risorgimento tradition, carried as fact by the English account.
stops.campa: The French land at Civitavecchia to restore the Pope and lay siege to Rome. Anita is in the city through it, near the front in Trastevere, working among the wounded legionaries. That she rode among the defenders in male dress and fought on the walls comes down as tradition and nothing firmer; the Italian account gives her the hospital and not the parapet, and both versions stay in circulation. The monument Rome eventually raises to her will choose the horse and the pistol. She is pregnant with a fifth child.
suggested_refs: The field hospitals of Trastevere during the French siege of Rome, 1849

stops.name: Gianicolo, the wall carried
stops.date_confidence: attested: the French carried the Janiculum in the night of 29-30 June and the Assembly voted to end resistance on 30 June; French troops entered Rome on 3 July and it.wikipedia dates the Republic's end 4 July 1849. The commonly repeated fall on 29 June conflates the three.
stops.campa: The French carry the Janiculum in the night of the twenty-ninth to the thirtieth of June, after two months of assault on the western wall. On the thirtieth the Assembly votes to end resistance; on the third of July French troops enter the city. Anita is in Rome for all of it. Eighty-three years later her bones will be brought back up to this same ridge by a special train and set under a bronze horse a few hundred metres from where the wall was broken, by a government that was not born when she died.
suggested_refs: The breached western wall of Rome on the Janiculum, June 1849

stops.name: Rome, the march out
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia 'Giuseppe Garibaldi' gives the withdrawal from Rome with 4,000 troops on 1-2 July 1849.
stops.campa: Garibaldi rides out of Rome with about four thousand volunteers, refusing both surrender and a safe passage into exile, intending to reach Venice, which is still holding against Austria. Anita rides with the column. She is pregnant with a fifth child and already ill; she is offered a way out and does not take it. Four armies, French, Austrian, Spanish and Neapolitan, close on the retreat from four directions before it has cleared the Campagna. Nothing about the plan is realistic and the column marches anyway.
suggested_refs: The muster of the retreating legion outside the Lateran, 2 July 1849

stops.name: Tivoli, into the hills
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the column's passage through Tivoli in the first days of July is taken from the route of the retreat; no source consulted names Anita at this stop, and the day is inferred.
stops.campa: The column turns east into the hills at Tivoli, above the falls of the Aniene, doubling and feinting to keep the French cavalry from fixing it in place. This is the pattern of the whole month: no battle offered, no town held, the road chosen for wherever the enemy is not. Anita rides in the middle of it, sick with a fever nobody yet names, through a country she reached eighteen months ago and cannot ask directions in. The legion is already shedding men at every halt.
suggested_refs: The route of Garibaldi's retreat from Rome through Tivoli and the Apennines

stops.name: City of San Marino, the legion released
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia 'Giuseppe Garibaldi' dates the arrival in San Marino to 31 July 1849 with roughly 250 men remaining.
stops.campa: Reduced to about two hundred and fifty men, the column crosses into the neutral republic of San Marino and Garibaldi releases his followers from their oath, dissolving the legion rather than let it be destroyed on the road. The Austrians ring the little state and demand them. That night he leaves with the few who refuse release, and Anita is among them. She is offered, for the second time in a month, a way to stop, on the ground that she is dying, and for the second time she does not take it.
suggested_refs: The convent of the Capuchins at San Marino, where the legion was dissolved

stops.name: Cesenatico, thirteen fishing boats
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia 'Giuseppe Garibaldi' dates the requisition of thirteen bragozzi at Cesenatico to 1 August 1849.
stops.campa: They come down to the Adriatic at Cesenatico in the night and requisition thirteen bragozzi, the flat-bottomed fishing boats of the coast, with their crews. Two hundred men put to sea for Venice, up a coast the Austrian navy patrols. Anita is carried aboard. The corsair of the Lagoa dos Patos is at sea again, ten years and one ocean from Laguna, in borrowed fishing boats, running for a republic that will surrender three weeks after he stops trying to reach it.
suggested_refs: The port canal of Cesenatico, designed by Leonardo, from which the bragozzi sailed

stops.name: Off Comacchio, the Austrian squadron
stops.date_confidence: contested: en.wikipedia dates the interception 2 August, while it.wikipedia puts the landing near Magnavacca on 3 August, which places the interception on the night of 2-3 August. Both datings are left standing.
stops.campa: An Austrian squadron finds the flotilla in the night off the Comacchio coast. Most of the boats are taken or driven onto the beach and their crews captured; the men in them are shot or imprisoned in the days that follow. One boat gets clear in the confusion, and it is the one carrying Garibaldi and Anita. She is by now unable to stand unaided. The expedition to relieve Venice ends about fifty hours after it began, and what is left of it is two people in a fishing boat off a hostile shore.
suggested_refs: The Austrian Adriatic squadron's interception of the Cesenatico flotilla

stops.name: Magnavacca, carried ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia to 3 August 1849. Coordinates from it.wikipedia 'Porto Garibaldi'; the widely copied pair 44.6844, 12.2853 falls in open water some kilometres offshore.
stops.campa: The boat grounds near Magnavacca, a fishing hamlet on the sand at the mouth of the Comacchio lagoons. Garibaldi carries Anita ashore into country patrolled by Austrian troops with orders to shoot him, and Colonel Gioacchino Bonnet takes charge of getting him away. In 1919 the hamlet is renamed Porto Garibaldi for what happened on this beach. The renaming keeps his name and not hers, though it was she who was carried up it. She is twenty-seven days from her twenty-eighth birthday.
suggested_refs: The beach at Porto Garibaldi, renamed from Magnavacca on 13 April 1919

stops.name: Sant'Alberto, across the Reno
stops.date_confidence: attested that the fugitives sheltered at Sant'Alberto, with Ugo Bassi, Giovanni Livraghi and G. B. Culiolo named by it.wikipedia; the Ravaglia family name specifically does not appear in that article. Coordinates from it.wikipedia 'Sant'Alberto (Ravenna)'.
stops.campa: They cross the Reno near Sant'Alberto, moving through reed marshes with local republicans guiding them: Ugo Bassi, Giovanni Livraghi and Giovanni Battista Culiolo are in the party or close to it. Anita is carried the last stages. Every household that touches this flight is risking a firing squad for it, and she is handed along the marsh from one hiding place to the next, in the direction of a farm inland where there is a bed. What she said on this crossing, if she said anything, is recorded by none of the men who were carrying her.
suggested_refs: The Reno crossing at Sant'Alberto and the Romagnol republicans who guided the flight

stops.name: Fattoria Guiccioli, Mandriole: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested: 4 August 1849 at 7:45 pm, Guiccioli farm, Mandriole. Cause of death is contested: en.wikipedia and it.wikipedia give malaria, pt.wikipedia gives typhoid fever. Coordinates from it.wikipedia 'Mandriole'; two different wrong pairs circulate for this spot.
stops.campa: She is carried into the Guiccioli farmhouse at Mandriole and dies there at a quarter to eight in the evening, with the fifth child unborn. The English and Italian accounts give malaria; the Portuguese gives typhoid. Garibaldi takes her pulse, finds none, and is moved on within minutes because Austrian troops are close. He is forty-two. He has lost Rome, the legion, the republic and now her inside five weeks, and he has thirty-three years left in which to be called the hero of two worlds.
stops.quote: I felt most deeply self-reproach on that day when, at the mouth of the Po, having landed, in our retreat from an Austrian squadron, while still hoping to restore her to life, on taking her pulse I found her a corpse, and sang the hymn of despair. I prayed for forgiveness, for I thought of the sin of taking her from her home.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, autobiographical sketch, in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (1861), Ch. IX, written in 1850, months after her death, and inserted as a retrospective aside inside the 1839 meeting narrative
suggested_refs: The Fattoria Guiccioli at Mandriole, preserved as a Garibaldian memorial
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

segments.name: The Graves, and the Uses of Her

stops.name: Mandriole, buried in the sand
stops.date_confidence: attested: the hasty concealed burial at the motta della Pastorara is given by it.wikipedia and en.wikipedia, on the day of death or immediately after.
stops.campa: The people who sheltered them bury her at once and in secret, in sand at the place called the motta della Pastorara, without rites and without a marker, so that the Austrians and the papal police cannot find the body. She is twenty-seven. She has been in Italy nineteen months, at war for the last six of them, and she goes into the ground with nothing written over her and nobody left standing beside it. Six days later children playing on the dune find the remains uncovered, and every burial she is given after this one is arranged by other people, for their own reasons.
suggested_refs: The motta della Pastorara, first burial place, near Mandriole

stops.name: Mandriole cemetery, the accusation and the sketch
stops.date_confidence: attested: reburial in the Mandriole cemetery on 10 August 1849. The strangulation allegation and its retraction are reconstruction assembled across the English, Italian and Portuguese articles and are carried as [R].
stops.campa: The body is recovered and buried properly in the local cemetery. Papal investigators examining it allege marks of strangulation, and the family who sheltered her stand accused of killing her; ecclesiastical medical examiners later put the marks down to decomposition and the accusation collapses. The next year, on Staten Island, Garibaldi begins writing his own life for an American translator, and sends the sketch of Anita first, ahead of his own.
stops.quote: According to what I have promised you, I send you the first biographical sketch; and do not be surprised that it is that of my wife. She was my constant companion, in good and bad fortune—sharing, as you will see, my greatest dangers, and surpassing the bravest men.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, letter to Theodore Dwight, Staten Island, 30 October 1850, prefacing The Life of General Garibaldi (trans. Dwight, 1861)
suggested_refs: The Mandriole parish cemetery, second burial place
sources: Project Gutenberg ebook 50544, The Life of General Garibaldi

stops.name: Cimetière du Château, Nice: the third grave
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia to 11 November 1859. Coordinates from fr.wikipedia for the Cimetière du Château; the pair 43.6959, 7.2716 in circulation lands in Vieux Nice, not the cemetery.
stops.campa: Ten years on, patriots led by her friend Giuseppe Deideri exhume the remains and carry them to Nice, to a chapel in the cemetery on the castle hill, above the town where her children were raised by their grandmother. The Portuguese account says she was exhumed seven times across these decades; the Italian and English accounts describe fewer moves and the tally is not corroborated. Within a year Nice is ceded to France and Garibaldi loses the town he was born in.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the Cimetière du Château, Nice, third burial place

stops.name: Staglieno, Genoa: waiting for the state
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1931 by it.wikipedia; no day is given and the date defaults to the first. Coordinates from it.wikipedia for the Cimitero monumentale di Staglieno.
stops.campa: The remains are exhumed again and placed for the time being in the pantheon of the monumental cemetery of Staglieno, above Genoa, while Rome prepares a state ceremony. Genoa is the city the Thousand sailed from, at Quarto on its eastern shore, where Gabriele D'Annunzio stood in May 1915 before the monument to that expedition and spoke his country into a war. The Fascist state is by then assembling the Risorgimento into its own ancestry, and it has decided that it wants her.
suggested_refs: The Pantheon of the Cimitero monumentale di Staglieno, Genoa

stops.name: Gianicolo, the bronze horse
stops.date_confidence: attested: it.wikipedia 'Monumento ad Anita Garibaldi' gives arrival in Rome by special train on 2 June 1932 and inauguration on 4 June 1932. The 2 December 1932 date carried by it.wikipedia's biography article, and widely copied, is an error for 2 giugno.
stops.campa: A special train brings her into Rome on the second of June; on the fourth the monument is inaugurated and the remains are sealed into its base. Mario Rutelli has cast her on a rearing horse, a pistol in her right hand, the infant Menotti held in her left arm. Benito Mussolini presides and speaks. Delegations from ten nations attend, Brazil and Uruguay among them. She is back on the ridge she stood on in June 1849, and the regime that put her there is using her to say something about itself.
suggested_refs: Mario Rutelli's equestrian Monumento ad Anita Garibaldi, Gianicolo, inaugurated 4 June 1932

stops.name: Laguna, the museum in the old jail
stops.date_confidence: attested that the building was designated for museum use on 31 July 1949, for the centenary of her death; pt.wikipedia dates the actual inauguration of the museum to 1956, so the opening claim often made for 1949 overstates the record.
stops.campa: In Laguna the eighteenth-century chamber-and-jail building where the República Juliana was proclaimed over her head in 1839 is set aside as a museum in her name on the centenary of her death, and opened in 1956. It holds Farroupilha arms, period furnishings, effects said to be hers and Giuseppe's, and an urn of soil brought from her burial place near Ravenna. The empire she fought is now the republic that claims her, and it keeps a jar of Italian earth in the old jail to prove it.
suggested_refs: The Museu Anita Garibaldi in the Edifício de Câmara e Cadeia, Laguna, listed by IPHAN

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the retellings
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Unidos do Viradouro enredo parades in 1999 and places third; Flávio Aguiar's novel Anita takes the Jabuti in 2000. The date defaults to the first of the carnival year.
stops.campa: The samba school Unidos do Viradouro parades her through the Sambódromo as its enredo and finishes third; the next year Flávio Aguiar's novel Anita takes the Jabuti prize. On screen she is played by Anna Magnani in Camicie Rosse in 1952, by Giovanna Antonelli in A Casa das Sete Mulheres in 2003, by Valeria Solarino in an Italian miniseries in 2012, and by Ana Paula Arósio in a Brazilian film in 2013. Two countries keep remaking her, and neither one concedes her to the other.
suggested_refs: The 1999 Unidos do Viradouro enredo on Anita Garibaldi; Camicie Rosse (1952)

stops.name: Brasília, the Book of Heroes
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 2012 by pt.wikipedia, citing Law 12.615; no day is given and the date defaults to the first.
stops.campa: Law 12.615 inscribes her name in the Livro dos Heróis e Heroínas da Pátria, kept in the Pantheon of Liberty and Democracy in Brasília. Two municipalities in Santa Catarina already carry her name, Anita Garibaldi and Anitápolis; there is a bust in Belo Horizonte, an avenue in Salvador, a street in Joinville, and a monument at Morrinhos, in what is now Tubarão, on the ground where she lived. A republican rebel against the Brazilian Empire has become Brazilian state canon by act of parliament.
suggested_refs: Lei 12.615 de 2012 and the Livro dos Heróis e Heroínas da Pátria, Brasília
